```{r}
#| label: setup
#| message: false

library(tidyverse)
set.seed(222)
theme_set(theme_bw(22))

fmt <- \(x, digits = 2) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
pct <- \(x) paste0(round(100 * x), "%")

# ---- Lab 7: drinking water ----
pcthisp_breaks <- c(0, 10, 25, 50, 100)
drinking_water <- read_csv("../data/drinking_water.csv") |>
  select(pwsid, pctpov, pcthisp, health, violation) |>
  mutate(
    pctpov_bin = cut(pctpov, seq(0, 100, by = 10), include.lowest = TRUE),
    pcthisp_bin = cut(pcthisp, pcthisp_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)
  )

pov_hisp_summary <- drinking_water |>
  summarize(
    pctpov = mean(pctpov),
    prop_violation = mean(violation),
    mean_health = mean(health),
    var_health = var(health),
    n = n(),
    .by = c(pctpov_bin, pcthisp_bin)
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 50)

additive_glm <- glm(
  violation ~ pctpov + pcthisp,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = drinking_water
)
interaction_glm <- glm(
  violation ~ pctpov * pcthisp,
  family = binomial(link = "logit"),
  data = drinking_water
)

lab7_grid <- expand_grid(
  pctpov = seq(0, 70, by = 1),
  pcthisp = c(5, 17.5, 37.5, 75)
) |>
  mutate(pcthisp_bin = cut(pcthisp, pcthisp_breaks, include.lowest = TRUE))
lab7_grid$additive_link <- predict(additive_glm, lab7_grid, type = "link")
lab7_grid$additive_p <- predict(additive_glm, lab7_grid, type = "response")
lab7_grid$interaction_p <- predict(
  interaction_glm,
  lab7_grid,
  type = "response"
)

int_b <- coef(interaction_glm)
int_slope <- \(hisp) int_b[["pctpov"]] + int_b[["pctpov:pcthisp"]] * hisp

comparison <- expand_grid(pctpov = 50, pcthisp = c(0, 75))
comparison$additive <- predict(additive_glm, comparison, type = "response")
comparison$interaction <- predict(
  interaction_glm,
  comparison,
  type = "response"
)

hisp_scale <- scale_color_viridis_d("% Hispanic")
lab7_axes <- labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "P(violation)")

# ---- Exotic bees ----
bees <- read_csv("../data/exotic-bees.csv") |>
  mutate(impervious = 100 * NLCD500m)

# ---- Overdispersion ----
pov_summary <- drinking_water |>
  summarize(
    mean_health = mean(health),
    var_health = var(health),
    n = n(),
    .by = pctpov_bin
  ) |>
  filter(n >= 10)
health_pois <- glm(
  health ~ pctpov * pcthisp,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = drinking_water
)
count_freqs <- tibble(count = 0:5) |>
  mutate(
    Observed = map_dbl(count, \(k) mean(drinking_water$health == k)),
    Poisson = map_dbl(count, \(k) mean(dpois(k, fitted(health_pois))))
  )
```

# Poisson regression

## Today's agenda

- **Recap** lab 7: the interaction (15 min)
- **Introduce** Poisson regression (15 min)
- **Calculate** exotic bee richness by hand (15 min)
- **Count** drinking water violations (25 min)
- **Discuss** overdispersion (10 min)

# Lab 7 recap

## Does poverty affect every community the same way?

Proportion of water systems with a health-based violation, binned by poverty and % Hispanic.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(
  pov_hisp_summary,
  aes(pctpov, prop_violation, color = pcthisp_bin)
) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n)) +
  geom_line() +
  hisp_scale +
  scale_size_area(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "Proportion with violation")
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

The slope is steepest in majority-Hispanic communities. That's what an interaction looks like.

:::

## The additive model

$$
\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PctPov} + \beta_2 \text{PctHisp}
$$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(lab7_grid, aes(pctpov, additive_p, color = pcthisp_bin)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = prop_violation), data = pov_hisp_summary) +
  hisp_scale +
  lab7_axes
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

No interaction term. So why aren't the lines parallel?

:::

## Parallel on the link scale

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(lab7_grid, aes(pctpov, additive_link, color = pcthisp_bin)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  hisp_scale +
  labs(x = "% below poverty", y = "logit(P(violation))")
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

The model is additive in **log odds**. The inverse logit is nonlinear, so the same change in log odds moves $p$ more when $p$ is closer to 0.5.

:::

## The interaction model

$$
\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PctPov} + \beta_2 \text{PctHisp} + \beta_3 \text{PctPov} \times \text{PctHisp}
$$

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(lab7_grid, aes(pctpov, interaction_p, color = pcthisp_bin)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.5) +
  geom_point(aes(y = prop_violation), data = pov_hisp_summary) +
  hisp_scale +
  lab7_axes
```

## What's the slope for poverty?

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}

Rearrange the linear part to group the PctPov terms:

$$
\text{logit}(p) = \beta_0 + \beta_2 \text{PctHisp} + (\beta_1 + \beta_3 \text{PctHisp}) \text{PctPov}
$$

:::

::: {.fragment}

| % Hispanic | Slope for poverty (log odds per point) |
|-----------:|:---------------------------------------|
| 0  | $\beta_1 =$ `r fmt(int_slope(0), 3)` |
| 75 | $\beta_1 + 75 \beta_3 =$ `r fmt(int_slope(75), 3)` |

:::

::: {.fragment}

- $\beta_3$ is positive and significant: poverty matters more as % Hispanic increases.

:::

## Why does it matter?

Predicted probability of a violation in a community where 50% of households are below the poverty line:

| % Hispanic | Additive | Interaction |
|-----------:|:--------:|:-----------:|
| 0  | `r pct(comparison$additive[1])` | `r pct(comparison$interaction[1])` |
| 75 | `r pct(comparison$additive[2])` | `r pct(comparison$interaction[2])` |

::: {.fragment}

The additive model forces poverty to have the same effect everywhere, so it understates the risk faced by poor, majority-Hispanic communities.

:::

# From "whether" to "how many"

## Does urbanization favor exotic bees?

Fitch et al. (2019) counted the **number of exotic bee species** at `r nrow(bees)` gardens and natural areas around Ann Arbor, Michigan.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

ggplot(bees, aes(impervious, exotic.richness)) +
  geom_point(
    #position = position_jitter(height = 0.1, width = 0, seed = 1),
    shape = 21,
    size = 3
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 0:8) +
  labs(
    x = "% impervious surface within 500 m",
    y = "Exotic bee species"
  )
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Counts are whole numbers, never negative, with no upper limit. Neither a normal nor a Bernoulli distribution fits.

:::

## What is a Poisson variable?

The number of events in a fixed amount of time or space. One parameter: $\lambda$, the **mean** (also the variance).

```{r}
#| fig-width: 12
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-align: center

expand_grid(lambda = c(0.5, 2, 5), k = 0:12) |>
  mutate(
    prob = dpois(k, lambda),
    lambda = factor(paste("λ =", lambda), levels = paste("λ =", c(0.5, 2, 5)))
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(k, prob)) +
  geom_col(fill = "cornflowerblue") +
  facet_wrap(~lambda) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 12, by = 2)) +
  labs(x = "Count", y = "Probability")
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Small $\lambda$: mostly zeros. Larger $\lambda$: more spread out, and closer to symmetric.

:::

## Which response is a Poisson variable?

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

**A.** Whether a water system had a violation this year

[**B.** The number of violations at a water system this year]{.fragment .highlight-green fragment-index=1}

**C.** The concentration of nitrate in a water sample (mg/L)

:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="font-size:0.75em"}

- A is binary: Bernoulli, logistic regression.
- B is a count with no fixed upper limit: Poisson.
- C is continuous: it can be 2.37 mg/L. Counts can't.

:::

## Logistic vs. Poisson regression

| | Logistic | Poisson |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Response | 0 or 1 | 0, 1, 2, ... |
| Distribution | $\text{Bernoulli}(p)$ | $\text{Poisson}(\lambda)$ |
| Parameter | $p$, between 0 and 1 | $\lambda$, greater than 0 |
| Link | $\text{logit}(p) = \log\left(\frac{p}{1-p}\right)$ | $\log(\lambda)$ |
| Inverse link | $p = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\text{logit}(p)}}$ | $\lambda = e^{\log(\lambda)}$ |
| `family` in R | `binomial(link = "logit")` | `poisson(link = "log")` |

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Both are **generalized linear models**: pick a distribution for the response, then link its parameter to a linear equation. Only the family and the link change.

:::

## Why the log link?

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

- $\lambda$ has to be positive. A straight line can go below 0.
- $\log$ turns $(0, \infty)$ into $(-\infty, \infty)$, just like logit turns $(0, 1)$ into $(-\infty, \infty)$.
- Adding on the log scale means **multiplying** on the count scale:

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.85em"}

$$
\lambda = e^{\beta_0 + \beta_1 x} = e^{\beta_0} \times \left(e^{\beta_1}\right)^x
$$

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Each 1-unit increase in $x$ multiplies the expected count by $e^{\beta_1}$. If $\beta_1 = -0.5$, then $e^{-0.5} = 0.61$, and the expected count falls 39% per unit.

:::

## Write the model

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{ExoticRichness} &\sim \text{Poisson}(\lambda) \\
\log(\lambda) &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{PctImpervious}
\end{aligned}
$$



::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Line 1: the number of exotic species at each site is Poisson, with mean $\lambda$. 

Line 2: the log of $\lambda$ changes linearly with impervious surface.

:::

::: {.fragment}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false

bee_glm <- glm(
  exotic.richness ~ impervious,
  family = poisson(link = "log"),
  data = bees
)
```

:::

## On your handout

::: {style="font-size:0.8em"}

Exotic bee species richness vs. impervious surface.

1. **Write** the model in statistical notation
2. **Draw** $\log(\lambda)$ vs. % impervious surface (the linear part)
3. **Calculate** $\lambda$ for 0, 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100% impervious surface
4. **Draw** $\lambda$ on top of the data
5. **Check** whether a Poisson is a good fit: mean and variance

:::

## One more look at your handout

::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.85em"}

- Each 20-point step changes $\log(\lambda)$ by the same amount ($20\beta_1$).
- On the count scale, each step **multiplies** $\lambda$ by the same amount ($e^{20\beta_1}$).
- The Poisson fits these data well: the variance and mean are similar. Will that be true for drinking water violations?

:::

# Counting violations

## Lab 7 again, with counts

The `health` column is the **number** of health-based violations each water system had that year.

::: {style="font-size:0.85em"}

- Lab 7: did a system have _any_ violations? `violation ~ ...`, binomial
- Today: _how many_ violations did it have? `health ~ ...`, Poisson

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.85em"}

Open [Poisson regression in R](../labs/week8_monday.qmd) and work through it with a partner. Same recipe: visualize, fit, predict.

:::

# Overdispersion

## The Poisson's strong assumption

Variance **equals** mean, _for a given value of the predictor_. Check within bins of poverty:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.8
#| fig-align: center

axis_lims <- c(0.1, 5)
ggplot(pov_summary, aes(mean_health, var_health)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), color = "cornflowerblue") +
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = 1,
    y = 0.6,
    label = "variance = mean",
    size = 6,
    hjust = 0
  ) +
  scale_size_area(guide = "none") +
  scale_x_log10(limits = axis_lims) +
  scale_y_log10(limits = axis_lims) +
  labs(
    x = "Mean violations in bin (log scale)",
    y = "Variance in bin (log scale)"
  )
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

In every bin, the variance is bigger than the mean (typically about `r round(median(pov_summary$var_health / pov_summary$mean_health))` times bigger). This is **overdispersion**: the counts vary more than a Poisson can explain. Most systems have zero violations, and a few have many.

:::

::: {.notes}

Why not just compare the overall mean and variance? Because the assumption is conditional: Var(Y | x) = E(Y | x). The overall variance also includes variation in λ across systems with different predictors, so it would overstate overdispersion (here, about 6x overall vs. about 4.5x within bins).

:::

## Too few zeros, too few big counts

```{r}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.5
#| fig-align: center

count_freqs |>
  pivot_longer(-count, names_to = "source", values_to = "freq") |>
  ggplot(aes(count, freq, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(position = "dodge") +
  scale_fill_manual(NULL, values = c("grey40", "cornflowerblue")) +
  labs(x = "Health-based violations", y = "Proportion of systems")
```

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.75em"}

Observed zeros: `r pct(count_freqs$Observed[1])`. Poisson predicts `r pct(count_freqs$Poisson[1])`. The Poisson spreads the counts too evenly.

:::

## What to do 

If you're modeling counts in your final project (or capstone, or after graduation...) and you find overdispersion:

::: {.incremental}

- Use a _negative binomial_ response instead of Poisson.

- Negative binomial variables are also counts, but they can be more dispersed (spread out) than Poisson.

- We can discuss the details if you need them this quarter!

:::

# Recap

## Key points

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

**What's a generalized linear model?**

Pick a distribution for the response. Link its parameter to a linear equation.

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

**How do we model counts?**

As a Poisson variable, where the log of the mean, $\log(\lambda)$, changes linearly with the predictors.

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

**How do we interpret the coefficients?**

On the log scale, they add. On the count scale, $e^{\beta}$ multiplies the expected count.

:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:0.8em"}

**How do we check a Poisson model?**

Within bins of the predictors, compare the variance to the mean. If the variance is bigger, the counts are overdispersed.

:::

## References

Giacomangeli, G. (2023). Does Urbanization Favor Exotic Species? _QUBES Educational Resources_. <https://doi.org/10.25334/KG7P-AD07> (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Switzer, D., & Teodoro, M. P. (2017). The color of drinking water: Class, race, ethnicity, and Safe Drinking Water Act compliance. _Journal AWWA_, 109(9), 40–45. <https://doi.org/10.5942/jawwa.2017.109.0128>
